concept: The late-1990s internet boom inflated on investment far ahead of profit, and when it burst the speculation died but the technology did not.

facts.claim: The NASDAQ Composite index peaked at 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000.
Between 1995 and its peak in March 2000, the NASDAQ Composite rose by 600%.
facts.note: Commonly misquoted as roughly 400%. Use 600% or say 'roughly sixfold'.

facts.claim: At its trough on 9 October 2002 the NASDAQ-100 had fallen to 1,114, down 78% from its peak.
facts.note: The source attributes this trough figure to the NASDAQ-100, not the Composite. Do not swap the two indices in narration.

facts.claim: By the end of the 2002 stock market downturn, stocks had lost $5 trillion in market capitalisation since the peak.
By November 2000 most internet stocks had declined 75% from their highs, wiping out $1.755 trillion in value.

misconceptions: That the Nasdaq rose 'about 400%' between 1995 and 2000 - the figure in the source is 600%.
Conflating the NASDAQ Composite with the NASDAQ-100; the peak and the trough figures come from different indices.
That the crash ended the internet economy, rather than repricing it - several of the era's companies survived and grew.

strategy.rationale: The topic is natively a before/after pair: identical companies valued two ways, and survivors sitting beside casualties. Contrast cases let 15 seconds carry the causal point - what changed was the pricing of belief, not the technology - without spending a slide on definitions.

next_topics.why: The brief establishes that it burst but not the mechanism; the trigger is the natural next question and is well documented.
Places the episode in a pattern the learner can reuse, rather than as a one-off piece of tech history.

next_topics.why: fact-05 and the survival of the technology point straight at this; it is the concrete payoff of the contrast the lesson sets up.
